http://www.aina.org/news/20260807125903..text: Assyrian Patriarch Makes First Visit to Romania for Syriac Studies Congress By Aurelian Iftimiu https://basilica.ro Posted 2026-08-07 17:59 GMT His Holiness Mar Awa III, Catholicos-Patriarch of the Assyrian Church of the East. His Holiness Mar Awa III, Catholicos-Patriarch of the Assyrian Church of the East, made his first-ever visit to Romania from August 3 to 7. According to a press release from the Levant Institute, the visit took place in conjunction with the 14th World Congress for Syriac Studies and the 12th International Conference on Christian Arabic Studies, organised by the Levant Institute and the Romanian Academy at the Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest. The Patriarch participated in the congress alongside His Grace Mar Paulus Benjamin, Bishop of Chicago and the Eastern United States of the Assyrian Church of the East. About Patriarch Mar Awa III His Holiness is the 122nd Catholicos-Patriarch of the Assyrian Church of the East and the first primate of the Church to have been born in the diaspora, in Chicago, United States. The press release noted that his life story reflects the experience of Middle Eastern Christians over the past few decades. "The story of Mar Awa III is the story of an entire generation of Eastern Christians who were compelled to rebuild their lives far from the lands where they were born and received the gift of faith, while preserving a heritage nearly two millennia old." "He is not only the Patriarch of an ancient Church, but also a man whose biography embodies the journey of an entire community: Mesopotamia, the diaspora, the preservation of identity, and the memory of an endangered heritage," the press release noted. A bridge between East and West According to the same source, Patriarch Mar Awa III is promoting dialogue among Churches, advocates for the protection of the Christian heritage of the Near East, and supports historic Christian communities affected by conflicts in recent decades. His Holiness holds a doctorate in theology from the Pontifical Oriental Institute in Rome and is regarded as one of the leading contemporary scholars of the Syriac tradition. He has authored numerous works on the theology and spirituality of the Assyrian Church of the East. In a message issued ahead of the event, Patriarch Mar Awa III highlighted Romania's role in fostering dialogue between East and West. "These events send a very powerful message from the heart of the European Union. Historically, this message serves as a bridge between East and West, and Romania is one of the few countries within the European Union well-positioned to fulfil this important role," His Holiness said. The World Congress for Syriac Studies and the International Conference on Christian Arabic Studies will bring together scholars and representatives from leading universities and research institutes worldwide, providing a forum for academic and intercultural dialogue dedicated to Syriac and Arabic Christian heritage. The Assyrian Church of the East The Assyrian Church of the East traces its origins to the ancient Syriac Christian communities of Mesopotamia and links its foundation to the preaching of the Holy Apostle Thomas and his disciples, Saints Addai and Mari. During the first centuries of Christianity, the Church carried out extensive missionary work, reaching from Persia to India, Central Asia, and China. Following the Third Ecumenical Council of Ephesus in 431, the Assyrian Church of the East separated from the Orthodox Church, as it did not accept the council's decisions. Today, the headquarters of the Assyrian Church of the East is located in Ankawa, near Erbil, Iraq, while its faithful are spread across the Middle East, Europe, North America, and Australia. https://www.classicalcalifornia.org/arti.text: Find Us on Social Media articles / Brahms Saturday Morning Car Tunes: Johannes Brahms Berni Schoenfield/Getty Images Brahms the pop star? His melodies show up in movies, cartoons, even pop songs, because he loved popular music too! Tune in this week for a lullaby, a Hungarian dance, student drinking songs, and Frank Sinatra. Listen to the episode! Bettmann/Getty Images Howdy, howdy, howdy! I’m Solomon Reynolds , and this is: Saturday Morning Car Tunes ! This morning… Born in 1833, Johannes Brahms was a German Romantic composer who came after Beethoven , Schubert , and Schumann . As a kid, people say he played the piano in sailors’ bars to help earn money for his family. The folk and popular music he played there shows up in his own compositions. His Piano Sonata No. 1, which you're listening to right now, was inspired by both Beethoven and folk songs. Brahms studied the musical past but also looked toward what the future could sound like. He pushed the boundaries of Classical forms through variations, taking a melody and playing it as many ways as he could imagine. These are his V ariations on a Theme by Handel , which he called his “favorite work.” But Brahms wasn’t just good at writing piano variations. He could also handle a whole orchestra. His Variations on a Theme by Haydn was the first orchestral piece where he combined everything he’d learned from older composers into something new, genuinely his own. Because Brahms loved and collected so many folk songs, he got really good at writing melodies. You’ve probably already heard his most famous one. Brahms never wrote an opera—he could never find a libretto, or story, he liked. But many think his G erman Requiem is his greatest work. Instead of writing it in the traditional Latin, Brahms set the text in German, although he said it could be just called a “human” requiem. Critics raved, and the piece made Brahms a major European composer. When Hungarian refugees passed through Germany, Brahms met the violinist Ede Reményi, who taught him about the Hungarian style, a mix of Hungarian and Romani musics. The third movement of Brahms' Violin Concerto is his greatest work in the Hungarian style and was featured in the 2007 film, There Will Be Blood . In fact, film, TV, and pop culture love Brahms’s Hungarian music. His Hungarian Dance No. 5 shows up all over the place: in a Looney Tunes cartoon, a Charlie Chaplin movie, and even an episode of The Simpsons . One reason pop culture loves Brahms’s music so much is that Brahms himself borrowed from the pop music of his day. When the University of Breslau offered him an honorary doctorate, Brahms wrote his Academic Festival Overture for the occasion. The piece is packed with half a dozen popular tunes and songs the students would recognize. Brahms’ four symphonies were milestones in German music, some of the most important pieces written in the 19th century. His Third Symphony reached a new level of form, balance, and coherence. The third movement was so good, Frank Sinatra wrote it into his song, “Take My Love.” Brahms! He's the bombs dot coms. I’m Solomon Reynolds.
